EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
2010 Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren Stirling Moss Emerges From Hiding, Has 32.9 Miles on the Clock
30 photos
Photo: RM Sotheby's
The final 2010 Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren Stirling Moss ever built has just come out of its hiding place to look for a new home. The ultra-exclusive, ultra-rare automobile is expected to fetch in excess of $6 million.
This Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren Stirling Moss was completed on December 22, 2009, as a 2010 model. It is number 75 of 75 units ever built as a tribute to Sir Stirling Moss’s career and his 1955 Mille Miglia victory. That run is considered one of the greatest drives in motor racing history.
With co-driver Denis Jenkinson in the passenger seat and driving a Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR , sporting the iconic racing number 722 (which designated their starting time of 7:22 AM), Moss, then 25, set an all-time speed record that was never broken before the race was permanently discontinued.
Moss completed the grueling, non-stop 992-mile loop on open public roads across Italy, starting and finishing in Brescia, northern Italy, in 10 hours, 7 minutes, and 48 seconds, averaging a staggering 97.96 mph (157.65 kph) and finishing with a massive 32-minute lead over Juan Manuel Fangio.
Photo: RM Sotheby's That is exactly what the Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren Stirling Moss honors. This final car of the series was commissioned by a member of the Kuwait Royal Family and features a completely bespoke specification, which sets it apart from the standard Crystal Laurite Silver models that dominated the 75-unit production run and positions it as a holy grail for collectors.
Car number 75 left the McLaren Technology Centre (MTC) in Woking, Surrey, England, bound for Switzerland as a closing chapter of the historic Mercedes-Benz and McLaren partnership, codenamed "Project 7." It was first registered on March 10, 2010. Later on, in 2024, it entered a private collection in the United States.
Finished in an exclusive Fire Opal Red, paint code 000U, instead of the standard silver, the car comes with a Silver Arrow red-leather interior with contrasting bespoke yellow stitching, wrapping custom wide, oversized seats in red and black leather.
Unlike the standard production McLaren Stirling Moss examples that used exposed carbon fiber, this example features unique, highly advanced composite material, Alutex aluminum, giving the cabin a bright, gleaming, metallic silver finish.
Photo: RM Sotheby's It is also one of only two McLaren Stirling Moss examples in existence to feature an audio system. The other one, finished in Rosso Corsa, belongs to the Royal Family of Jordan, because money can buy anything, even in a car designed without one.
The standard model was built as a hyper-minimalist, hardcore track speedster and was delivered from the factory completely stripped of creature comforts. There was no infotainment screen, no telephone connectivity, no navigation, and absolutely no radio or sound system.
Mercedes-Benz engineered it that way to maximize weight savings, and because the open cockpit design does not involve a roof, side windows, or a windshield , wind noise at speed is so violent that a conventional car radio would be basically unhearable.
There are, however, two tiny glass wind deflectors, designed to divert air over the cabin, but at high speed, they become pretty much useless. And speaking of speed, the Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren Stirling Moss is powered by the 5.4-liter supercharged AMG V8, which pumps out 641 horsepower (650 metric horsepower) and 605 pound-feet (820 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: RM Sotheby's That is what makes it flash from zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) in 3.4 seconds and all the way to a top speed of 220 mph (354 kph), aerodynamically limited due to the open-cockpit configuration. A five-speed automatic transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels.
High-performance Brembo carbon-ceramic brakes, assisted by a rear spoiler that acts as a 65-degree active airbrake, provide the stopping power. Exclusively on this final Chassis 75, the multi-piston brake calipers are finished in gold from the factory.
However, the owner did not enjoy all that performance much. The odometer of the car shows just 32.9 miles (53 kilometers), which is basically delivery mileage plus driving up and down the ramp of a trailer for maintenance over all these years.
The model was homologated and road-registered for the United States. It is actually believed to be the only SLR Stirling Moss in existence that has cleared standard federal safety and compliance roadblocks entirely, making it fully street-legal across America.
Photo: RM Sotheby's In 2024, it crossed the auction block via a Bonhams Cars Auction, where the hammer dropped at $3.5 million. Now, at the RM Sotheby’s Sealed Auction, scheduled to take place between November 25 and December 2, it is expected to fetch north of $6 million.
So far, the most expensive of its kind ever sold was sold in August 2024 via RM Sotheby’s in Tegernsee, Germany, for 3,355,000 euros, which translates to roughly $3,660,000. The car responsible for the record was a pristine, silver 2009 example with only 28 miles on the clock. The red example, however, might shatter that record before the end of the month.
